skill.name: Must or might: how strongly a writer commits
skill.why: Strong words like must push you. Weak words like might leave wiggle room.
skill.how: Find the must, should or might word. Ask: is it strong, medium or weak?

steps.say: Three signs at the pool. They all talk about hats.

show.nudge: Should is good advice. You could still say no. Which gives no choice?
Might means maybe. It's just possible. Which gives no choice?

steps.ask: Tap the sign that gives you no choice.
steps.win: Yes! Must is strong: no choice. Should is medium: good advice. Might is weak: just possible.

steps.say: These words also show how sure a writer is. Here are three forecasts.

show.nudge: Will is very sure. It leaves no doubt. Which is only a maybe?
Probably is fairly sure. Which one is only a maybe?

steps.ask: Tap the forecast that is least sure.
steps.win: Yes! Might is not very sure. Will is very sure. Probably is in the middle: fairly sure.

steps.say: Other words do the same jobs. Find the one that makes a rule.

show.nudge: Ought to is like should: good advice. That's medium.
May is like might: just possible. That's weak.

steps.win: Yes! 'Have to' makes a rule, just like must.

steps.say: Strong, medium and weak. Teachers call this high, medium and low modality.

show.nudge: Will is very sure. That's high modality.
Should is in the middle. That's medium modality.

steps.ask: Tap the word with low modality.
steps.win: Yes! Could is low modality. It's only possible.

steps.say: Careful! Must can do a second job. Listen.
show: Tully says: The lights are off. Gus

options.text: Gus has no choice. Sleeping is a rule.
options.reason: Is anyone giving Gus a rule? Tully is guessing from a clue: the lights.
Must is a strong word. How sure does Tully sound?

steps.win: Yes! Here must means very sure, not a rule. Must is strong either way.

steps.say: Careful! Big words sell. Small words hide in the small print.
steps.ask: How sure is the seller, really?

options.reason: Fairly sure is probably. The small print says may. That's weaker.
The big word is will. Now read the small print. What does may tell you?

steps.win: Yes! The tiny 'may' is the seller's way out. Always read the small print.

terms.means: Must, have to, will, definitely. No choice, or very sure. High modality.
Should, ought to, probably. Good advice, or fairly sure.
Might, could, may. Just possible, or not very sure. Low modality.

card.test: Find the must, should or might word. Is it a rule or a guess? How strong is it?

encounters.frame: Two letters about the old Bluster Rock jetty appeared in the local paper on the same day.
encounters.text: LETTER 1, from the Save Our Jetty group: The council must not knock down the old jetty. It has stood for a hundred years, and it will certainly stand for a hundred more if it is repaired. Without it, the fishing club will close, the tourists will vanish and the town will lose its heart. Every resident should come to the meeting on Thursday night and make their voice heard, because this decision cannot be undone. LETTER 2, from the council's engineer, Dana Whitlock: Our divers inspected the jetty last month and found rust in several of the main posts. Repairs might keep it safe for another ten years, although we can't be sure until more tests are done in February. It could also be cheaper to build a new jetty beside the old one, but we have not finished costing either option. The council will probably decide in March, after the full report is finished. We will publish every test result on the noticeboard outside the town hall, so that residents can read them for themselves. Both letters drew dozens of replies, and the meeting hall has been booked for an extra hour. The fishing club has painted a banner that says 'Hands Off Our Jetty' in letters a metre tall.

encounters.frame: A dusty painting turned up in a Bluster Rock shed. Indi read what four art experts said about it.
encounters.text: The painting shows a mob of galahs exploding off a red cliff at sunset, and it was found wrapped in a hessian sack behind an old ute. The sack also held a rusty paintbrush and a note that said only 'For M.' The owner of the shed, a retired truck driver named Col Burrows, said he had no idea how it got there. Some people believe it is a lost work by Marlo Quince, the famous painter who lived on Bluster Rock fifty years ago. She was known for painting birds in flight, and her work now hangs in galleries across the country. Four experts were asked to look at it. Dr Vale said, 'This painting is, without doubt, by Marlo Quince, because her thumbprint is pressed into the paint in the corner.' Mr Osei said, 'It is almost certainly hers, although the frame is newer than the painting.' Ms Brandt said, 'It might be hers, but it might just as easily be the work of one of her students.' Mr Hoyle said, 'It is highly unlikely to be hers, because she never painted on wooden board.' The Mightoo said nothing, but it did try to land on the painted galahs.
encounters.prompt: Put the experts in order, from the one most sure it IS a Marlo Quince to the one most sure it is NOT.
encounters.success: Without doubt, almost certainly, might, highly unlikely. Each expert commits a little less to it being hers.

items: Mr Hoyle: highly unlikely to be hers
body.reason: Without doubt is surest. Almost certainly is close behind. Might is only possible. Highly unlikely means probably not.

encounters.frame: The Mightoo found a camper's diary under a rock at Ghost Gum Gorge.
encounters.text: Day 1. We drove in along a dirt track so bumpy that my teeth rattled, and the gorge walls glowed orange in the late afternoon sun. Set up the tent beneath the biggest ghost gum in the gorge. Around midnight, I heard a slow scratching sound on the canvas, right beside my head. It might have been a possum, or it could have been nothing more than the wind dragging a branch across the tent. I didn't dare look. Day 2. This morning, there were small footprints in the dust outside the tent, each one about the size of a twenty-cent coin. They were probably made by a small animal, although the wind had blurred them too much to be sure. The scratching came back after dark, and this time I heard a soft thump on the roof. Day 3. When I woke up, the packet of marshmallows I'd left in my boot was torn open. There were tiny paw prints in the spilt sugar, and curled up asleep in the boot was a ringtail possum, its tail wrapped around the last marshmallow. So that's what the scratching was. It must be the possum. There's no other explanation, and it's still snoring. I've named it Marshmallow.
encounters.prompt: Why does the writer change from might and could to must?
encounters.success: Each day brings more evidence. By Day 3 the possum is in the boot, so the writer is sure.
